planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. LCP 85-384 was released from the joint LSU AgCenter/USDA-ARS sugarcane breeding program and for many years became the dominant commercial variety grown across the Louisiana sugar belt.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. LCP 85-384 (the LCP designation reflects its origin in the joint Louisiana-USDA sugarcane cooperative breeding program) rose to become the overwhelmingly dominant sugarcane variety in the Louisiana sugar industry for many years, prized for high early-season sugar yield, good cold tolerance for Louisiana's subtropical-to-temperate climate, and strong ratooning ability. It was later grown on well over half of the state's cane acreage before increasing disease pressure led growers to diversify into newer releases. Home growers can treat it like any heirloom cane: harvest in late fall after cool nights concentrate the sugars, strip the leaves, and press or chew the stalks fresh, or cook the juice into syrup. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically freezes back to the rhizome in hard winters and regrows from the root each spring.
sources: USDA-ARS Sugarcane Research Unit, Houma, Louisiana

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. HoCP 96-540 (the HoCP designation refers to the USDA-ARS sugarcane research station at Houma, Louisiana, working in cooperation with the LSU AgCenter) became one of the leading commercial varieties in the Louisiana sugar belt, succeeding earlier releases as growers shifted acreage to newer cultivars.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. HoCP 96-540 emerged from the Houma, Louisiana USDA-ARS/LSU AgCenter sugarcane breeding program and became a widely planted commercial variety across the Louisiana sugar belt, valued by growers for its yield and disease resistance relative to older releases. While bred for large-scale sugar production rather than dooryard use, home growers can treat it like any other cane: harvest in late fall after cool nights sweeten the stalks, strip the leaves, and press or chew the stalks fresh, or cook the juice into syrup. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.
sources: USDA-ARS Sugarcane Research Unit, Houma, Louisiana

common_name: Pele's Smoke Sugarcane (Dark Purple Ornamental Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Pele's Smoke is grown as an ornamental sugarcane for its very dark, smoky purple-black stalks rather than for sugar or syrup production.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Pele's Smoke is grown primarily as a dramatic ornamental grass for its deep, smoky purple-black stalk coloration, which darkens further with sun exposure and cool weather, creating a striking vertical accent in borders and large containers. Like other sugarcanes it can also be chewed fresh or pressed for juice, but it is chiefly valued in Gulf South gardens for foliage color rather than sweetness or yield. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically freezes back to the rhizome in hard winters in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. California Striped is grown as an ornamental grass for its distinctly striped stalks, which add strong vertical color and pattern to large borders, tropical-style plantings, and big containers. As with other sugarcanes the stalks can be chewed fresh or pressed for juice, but this type is chosen in Gulf South gardens mainly for its ornamental stalk pattern rather than for sweetness or yield. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.
